sec.title: Background
sec.p: Sacubitril/valsartan, an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor, influences metabolic pathways, potentially altering glycemic indices and lipid profiles, but evidence remains scattered. Therefore, we aimed to quantify changes in glycemic indices, lipid profiles, and uric acid with sacubitril/valsartan.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This study followed PRISMA guidelines and was registered on PROSPERO. We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies reporting within-group changes in metabolic parameters in adults receiving sacubitril/valsartan. Risk of bias was separately assessed for randomized clinical trials (RCTs) and non-RCTs. Whenever multiple populations from a single record were included in an outcome, a multilevel meta-analysis was used; otherwise, a conventional random-effects meta-analysis was applied.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Twenty-seven studies were included, involving a total of 11,093 participants. Meta-analysis showed significant reduction in hemoglobin A1c (MD -0.47%; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.75 to − 0.20), fasting blood glucose (MD -11.94 mg/dL; 95% CI -23.63 to -0.25), lowdensity lipoprotein (MD -12.1 mg/dL; 95% CI − 20.37 to -3.82), triglycerides (MD -21.95 mg/dL; 95% CI -40.02 to -3.88), total cholesterol (MD -17.08 mg/dL; 95% CI -32.38 to -1.78), highdensity lipoprotein (MD 2.21 mg/dL; 95% CI 0.91 to 3.5), uric acid (MD -0.41 mg/dL; 95% CI -0.80 to -0.01), but non-significant changes were observed in homeostatic model assessment index (MD -2.34; 95% CI: -4.83 to 0.14), and fasting plasma insulin (MD -4.03 µU/mL; 95% CI: -8.88 to 0.82). No publication bias was detected.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Sacubitril/valsartan provides modest but significant improvements across multiple glycemic and lipid parameters, supporting a favorable metabolic action in clinical practice in patients with heart failure.

sec.p: The study protocol was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) (CRD420251057875).

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Sacubitril/valsartan, a first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), has emerged as a pivotal therapeutic option across a growing spectrum of cardiovascular conditions [1]. It was primarily approved for managing heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), showing substantial benefits in lowering both mortality rates and hospital admissions [2]. Findings of the subsequent trials expanded the indication of sacubitril/valsartan for heart failure with mildly reduced (HFmrEF) or preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [3, 4], while its potential antihypertensive and renoprotective properties have also highlighted a promising role in the management of hypertension and chronic kidney disease (CKD) [5, 6].

The dual mechanism of action, combining neprilysin inhibition with blockade of the angiotensin II type-1 receptor, affects a wide range of physiological pathways beyond the isolated hemodynamic regulation [7]. Neprilysin regulates the degradation of several vasoactive and metabolic peptides, including natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), which are implicated in glycemic control, lipid metabolism, and energy balance. Consequently, sacubitril/valsartan may exert significant metabolic effects, both beneficial and adverse, that are not yet fully understood.

Although a growing number of clinical studies have investigated metabolic parameters in patients receiving sacubitril/valsartan, a comprehensive synthesis of the evidence is warranted to clarify the broader metabolic profile of this drug, particularly in populations with cardiometabolic comorbidities, such as obesity, diabetes, and CKD. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to assess the metabolic alterations associated with sacubitril/valsartan therapy, focusing on its effects on glycemic indices and lipid profiles, including high-density lipoprotein (HDL), low-density lipoprotein (LDL), triglyceride (TG), and total cholesterol (TC).

sec.title: Protocol and registration
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis was implemented in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [8], and the study protocol was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) (CRD420251057875) [9].

sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p: A thorough literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, without restriction by publication country, from inception to July 2025. The following search terms were used to identify and extract the relevant records: ((“sacubitril” OR “Entresto” OR “LCZ696” OR “sacubitril-valsartan” OR “sacubitril/valsartan” OR “angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor” OR “ARNI”) AND (“metabolic” OR “metabolism” OR “lipid” OR “lipoprotein” OR “HDL” OR “high-density lipoprotein” OR “LDL” OR “low-density lipoprotein OR “triglyceride” OR “TG” OR “total cholesterol OR “TC” OR “glucose” OR “blood sugar” OR “glycemia” OR “HbA1c” OR “glycated hemoglobin” OR “A1C” OR “diabetes” OR “insulin sensitivity” OR “insulin resistance”)). Our search across all databases was restricted to these terms in the title and abstract. Moreover, references of the included studies were further screened for potential additional studies.

sec.title: Eligibility criteria
sec.p: The PICO approach was incorporated in screening and selecting the appropriate studies. According to the PICO scheme, the framework of this study was: population: patients receiving sacubitril/valsartan regardless of the condition; intervention: sacubitril/valsartan consumption; comparison: baseline values of the metabolic indices; outcome: follow-up values of the metabolic indices, namely, TG, HDL, LDL, TC, fasting blood sugar (FBS), hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), and insulin resistance markers (no restriction was set for the measurement methods). Observational, retrospective, and prospective cohort studies and clinical trials reporting baseline and follow-up values of the metabolic indices were considered eligible for inclusion in the study. Meeting abstracts, editorials, case reports, case series, animal studies, in vivo and in vitro investigations, and non-English records were excluded.

sec.title: Study selection and data extraction
sec.p: The study screening and selection process was conducted independently by two reviewers (A.P.A., F.A.), with discrepancies resolved through consultation with the third reviewer and joint discussion (P.R.). After removing duplicate records, an initial screening of the remaining articles was conducted by reviewing their titles and abstracts for relevance. Studies deemed potentially eligible and relevant underwent full-text assessment to verify their suitability for inclusion. In cases where the full text is unavailable, we attempted to contact the corresponding authors to request the manuscript, if feasible. Titles/abstracts and full-text articles were independently screened by two investigators; disagreements were resolved by consultation with a third reviewer. Inter-rater agreement for full-text inclusion was very good (Cohen’s κ = 0.91). The entire process was carried out using EndNote version 20.

If multiple sub-analyses of a single trial were available, preference was given to those with longer follow-up periods and larger included populations. A pre-designed structured table consisting of the first author’s name, publication date, study location, patients’ demographics and conditions, study design, sample size, follow-up period, and baseline and follow-up values of the metabolic indices was used to aid in the extraction process. In case of incomplete data, efforts were made to contact the corresponding authors of the studies.

sec.title: Quality assessment
sec.p: For randomized controlled trials (RCTs), the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (RoB 2.0) was utilized to assess biases in randomization, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting [10]. Although only data from the sacubitril/valsartan group were pooled, the overall risk of bias was critically appraised, as flaws in randomization or design could indirectly influence outcomes of the intervention arm. In cohort studies, the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) was used to evaluate the selection, comparability, and outcome assessment domains, assigning an overall score of 0–9 [11]. Two reviewers independently conducted the assessments (F.A., M.F.).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Following common practice in the absence of reported within-person correlations, we conservatively assumed a pre–post correlation coefficient of r = 0.5 for all metabolic parameters. While HbA1c and other metabolic parameters measurements typically demonstrate higher test-retest correlations, this conservative estimate was chosen to ensure a more robust analysis that would not overstate the intervention effect and to produce wider, more robust confidence intervals. Whenever multiple populations were included and reported for an outcome, a multilevel (three-level) meta-analysis was used to account for the hierarchical (nested) data structure. Otherwise, conventional meta-analysis was applied to pool the measures. The three levels were defined as:

list-item.p: Level 1: sampling variance of each individual effect size
Level 2: variance among effect sizes within the same study (multiple arms)

sec.p: The three-level model was fitted using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation via the rma.mv() function with Knapp–Hartung adjustment for standard errors (test = “t” argument in the rma.mv() function). To investigate whether a three-level model better represents the data’s variability than a two-level model, we conducted a meta-analysis, setting the variance component at one level to zero, and compared the models. The ANOVA function was used to compare the models based on Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) values, and the significance of the likelihood ratio test. I2 statistics were used to assess heterogeneity across the published studies. However, given substantial methodological, individual, and setting variability and heterogeneity across the studies, a random-effects meta-analysis was used to pool the MDs. In the multilevel meta-analysis, we reported two I2 values: one attributable to within-cluster effect size differences and the other to between-cluster variation. We further performed a subgroup analysis, including only records on HF patients to reduce heterogeneity and enhance the robustness of our findings. Meta-regression analysis was used to explore potential sources of bias; however, this analysis was performed only for HbA1c MD due to the small number of studies reporting MD for other indices. To assess potential publication bias, Begg’s test was employed, and a funnel plot was depicted for visual evaluation, provided the number of included studies allowed for these analyses. All statistical analyses were conducted using R software (version 4.5.1), with a significance threshold set at p-value < 0.05.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: The initial database search identified 1184 studies. After excluding 299 duplicates, 885 records remained for title and abstract screening. From these, 72 articles were selected for eligibility assessment. The following full-text evaluation of 27 studies (12 RCTs and 15 observational studies) met the inclusion criteria. These studies, published between 2017 and 2024, were conducted in different geographical regions. The PRISMA flow chart depicts the study selection process of our study (Fig. 1).

caption.p: Prisma flow diagram demonstrating study selection

sec.title: Study characteristics
sec.p: The 27 included studies comprised a total of 11,093 participants, with a mean age of 64.5. Among studies reporting gender distribution, 37.2% of participants were females. The follow-up periods for these studies ranged from 2 months to 36 months. Although HF was the primary focus, several studies included participants with comorbid conditions, including hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Of the included records, 20 studies reported MDs for HbA1c, 11 for FBS, 12 for lipid parameters, 9 for serum uric acid, and 6 for insulin resistance markers. Detailed characteristics of the studies are demonstrated in Additional file 1.

sec.title: Pooled analysis of HbA1c difference
sec.p: Multilevel meta-analysis of MDs of HbA1c values before and after receiving sacubitril/valsartan from 20 studies and 22 subpopulations showed significantly decreased levels of HbA1c (pooled MD of -0.47%; 95% CI: -0.75, -0.20) (Fig. 2). The anova test revealed better performance of the three-level model, with lower AIC and BIC, but an insignificant likelihood ratio test (LRT) (AIC of 39.53 vs. 40.45 and BIC of 42.5 vs. 42.6; LRT of 2.91, p-value: 0.08). The estimated variance components were sigma2level 3 = 0.321 and sigma2level 2 = 0.017, which means that I2level 3 = 90.7% of the total variation can be attributed to between-cluster, and I2level 2 = 5% to within-cluster heterogeneity. The 95% prediction interval ranged from − 1.71% to 0.77%, indicating that although the pooled estimate suggests a modest glycemic benefit, the true effect could vary widely from a meaningful reduction of nearly 2% to no change or even slight worsening. The moderators investigated in the meta-regression were the percentage of female participants and the follow-up duration (in months). The moderator effects were minimal and insignificant. Female percentage yielded an estimate of -0.001 (95% CI: -0.0149 to 0.0116, p-value = 0.81), indicating no association with the effect size per percentage increase in female participants. Follow-up duration showed an estimate of -0.0007 (95% CI: -0.0294 to 0.0279, p-value = 0.95), indicating that the glycemic benefit of sacubitril/valsartan does not meaningfully increase or decrease with longer follow-up duration in the included studies. We repeated the analysis on the population of HF patients, and the results remained a significant decrease of HbA1c value following sacubitril/valsartan consumption (pooled MD = -0.42%; 95% CI: -0.66, -0.17) (Fig. 3).

sec.title: Pooled analysis of FBS difference
sec.p: As shown in the forest plot, the pooled MD of FBS before and after treatment with sacubitril/valsartan across 11 studies was − 11.94 mg/dL (95% CI: -23.63, -0.25; p-value = 0.046), which was statistically significant (Fig. 4). It is noteworthy that high heterogeneity was observed among the included studies (I2 = 97.73%, p-value < 0.0001). To reduce bias introduced by pooling data across diverse populations, a subgroup analysis was performed, including only studies of patients with HF. A meta-analysis of the seven studies yielded a larger and statistically significant decrease in FBS levels (pooled MD = -16.68 mg/dL; 95% CI: -33.11, -0.25; p-value = 0.047) (Fig. 5).

Pooled mean differences of fasting blood sugar values in patients with heart failure

sec.title: Pooled analysis of lipid parameters’ difference
sec.p: To evaluate the effect of sacubitril/valsartan on lipid levels, data on TC, LDL, HDL, and TG before and after sacubitril/valsartan were derived from 7, 9, 10, and 10 studies, respectively. As shown in Fig. 6, pooled MD for TC was reduced by -17.08 mg/dL (95% CI: -32.38, -1.78; p-value = 0.03), indicating a statistically significant difference. The meta-analysis of studies reporting LDL levels following sacubitril/valsartan use yielded a pooled MD of -12.1 mg/dL (95% CI: -20.37, -3.82; p-value = 0.009) (Fig. 7). Moreover, treatment with sacubitril/valsartan was associated with a significant increase in HDL levels (pooled MD of 2.21 mg/dL (95% CI: 0.91, 3.50; p-value = 0.004) (Fig. 8). As demonstrated in Figs. 9 and 10, the pooled MD of TG levels before and after treatment with sacubitril/valsartan was − 21.95 mg/ dL (95% CI: -40.02, -3.38; p-value = 0.02) in all included studies and − 22.85 mg/dL (95% CI: -43.2, -2.51; p-value = 0.03) in HF patients. Subgroup analyses in patients with HF were not conducted for studies reporting outcomes on TC, HDL, and LDL, as all enrolled patients had HF. Across all lipid-related outcomes, the results for heterogeneity were substantial. I2 values for TC, LDL, HDL, and TG were 92.3%, 87% 81.58% and 97.3%, respectively (all p-values < 0.001), indicating high variability among studies.

sec.title: Pooled analysis of uric acid difference
sec.p: A meta-analysis of the eight studies reporting changes in serum uric acid revealed a pooled MD of -0.41 mg/dL (95% CI: -0.8, -0.01; p-value = 0.04), suggesting a slight but statistically significant decrease in uric acid levels following treatment with sacubitril/valsartan (Fig. 11). A similar pattern was observed in HF patients (pooled MD = -0.43 mg/dL; 95% CI: -0.88, 0.03; p-value = 0.06), although it became statistically insignificant (Fig. 12). A considerable heterogeneity existed across the included studies, with an I2 of 96%.

sec.title: Pooled analysis of insulin resistance difference
sec.p: Insulin resistance was demonstrated as homeostatic model assessment (HOMA) index in three records. Accordingly, aggregated MDs of HOMA index from three studies indicated an insignificant decrease after the follow-up period (pooled MD = -2.34; 95% CI: -4.83, 0.14) (Fig. 13). Insulin sensitivity was further assessed in these studies, in addition to the study by Jordan et al. [12] and Ishibashi et al. [13], through the measurement of fasting plasma insulin, which our combined analysis showed similar results to HOMA index (pooled MD = -4.03; 95% CI: -8.88, 0.82) (Fig. 14).

sec.title: Publication bias
sec.p: Publication bias was formally assessed only for HbA1c and FBS, the only outcomes with sufficient numbers of included studies to allow meaningful testing. For HbA1c and FBS, visual inspection of the funnel plots (Figs. 15 and 16) showed reasonable symmetry, and Begg’s rank correlation test did not indicate statistically significant bias (p-value = 0.53 and 0.76, respectively). For all remaining outcomes, fewer than 10 studies contributed data per outcome, and formal statistical tests for publication bias were not performed. Consequently, the presence or absence of publication bias for these outcomes could not be reliably evaluated.

sec.title: Quality assessment
sec.p: The included studies underwent a thorough evaluation of quality and bias according to their designs. As detailed in Tables 1 and 2, neither the RoB 2.0 tool nor the NOS scores identified any study with a high risk of bias or poor quality.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of 27 studies including 11,093 participants, we observed that consumption of sacubitril/valsartan was associated with a consistent reduction in HbA1c (MD -0.47%; 95% CI -0.75 to − 0.20) and FBS (MD -11.94 mg/dL; 95% CI -23.63 to -0.25). Statistically significant improvements were also observed in other metabolic indices, including TC (MD -17.08 mg/dL; 95% CI -32.38 to -1.78), LDL (MD -12.1 mg/dL; 95% CI − 20.37 to -3.82), TG (MD -21.95 mg/dL; 95% CI -40.02 to -3.88), HDL (MD 2.21 mg/dL; 95% CI 0.91 to 3.5), and uric acid (MD -0.41 mg/dL; 95% CI -0.80 to -0.01). Trends toward improved insulin resistance indices (HOMA index, fasting plasma insulin) were observed but did not reach statistical significance.

To our knowledge, this is the first meta-analysis to evaluate the metabolic outcomes of sacubitril/valsartan on metabolic parameters. Earlier evidence was primarily derived from post hoc analyses of trials and several prospective studies, showing variable reductions in HbA1c and occasional lipid improvements, but results have been inconsistent and limited by small group sizes or short follow-up. Our findings, while more precise due to a larger cumulative sample size and multilevel modeling, must still be interpreted cautiously in light of substantial heterogeneity that was not fully explained by follow-up duration or sex distribution.

The reduction in HbA1c observed in our meta-analysis aligns with previous findings from major ARNI trials. Post-hoc analyses of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF demonstrated modest but significant HbA1c reductions among patients with diabetes, as well as a lower likelihood of progression to insulin therapy [14, 15]. Our pooled estimate (-0.47%) is slightly larger, reflecting inclusion of diverse real-world cohorts, including diabetic and prediabetic populations, and both short- and long-term follow-up. Despite differences in study design, location, and patient demographics, the consistent direction of effect supports the reproducibility and external validity of the HbA1c reduction. Although the mean change approaches the 0.5% minimal clinically important difference, the lower bound of the confidence interval falls below this threshold, limiting the conclusiveness of the findings [16].

The results of the primary studies regarding lipid values were generally inconsistent. For LDL, all point estimates favored a reduction, although the effect was not statistically significant in some individual studies. For TC, HDL, and TG, the direction of effect was inconsistent across studies, reflecting variability in baseline lipid levels, follow-up duration, and concomitant lipid-lowering therapy. By pooling these data, our meta-analysis detected statistically significant changes in LDL, TC, HDL, and TG, demonstrating that sacubitril/valsartan exerts modest but potentially beneficial effects on lipid profiles despite heterogeneity and limited power in individual studies. Nonetheless, the clinical relevance of these changes remains limited due to the modest magnitude and between-study heterogeneity.

Several mechanisms may underlie the metabolic improvements observed with sacubitril/valsartan. Neprilysin inhibition increases circulating natriuretic peptides, which stimulate adipose tissue lipolysis, enhance lipid mobilization, promote energy expenditure, and increase renal uric acid excretion, providing an explanation for the modest improvements in lipid parameters and uric acid [17, 18]. Natriuretic peptides also enhance peripheral insulin sensitivity and skeletal muscle glucose uptake, which may contribute to reductions in HbA1c and fasting glucose [19]. In addition, both neprilysin and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) degrade GLP-1, and in vivo studies suggest that neprilysin deficiency may even reduce DPP-4 activity, providing another pathway through which ARNI therapy could enhance GLP-1 [20]. Moreover, recent human data show that sacubitril/valsartan significantly enhances active GLP-1 concentrations when co-administered with a DPP-4 inhibitor, highlighting possible synergistic mechanism [21]. While these GLP-1 effects did not produce measurable glycemic changes in healthy individuals, another cohort of HF patients found that the increase in GLP-1 following sacubitril/valsartan therapy was associated with a decrease in fructosamine, regardless of the presence of diabetes [22]. The evidence supports the biological plausibility that natriuretic peptide pathways, improved insulin sensitivity, reduced DPP-4 activity, and incretin signaling collectively contribute to the metabolic profile observed in our meta-analysis.

In our meta-analysis, neither HOMA nor fasting plasma insulin reached statistical significance. This is likely attributable to the small number of eligible primary studies and the limited statistical power. In addition, we assumed a correlation coefficient (r) of 0.5 to compute the SD of change [21]. While this is a commonly used and acceptable assumption, it may widen confidence intervals, contributing to the non-significant findings.

Our meta-analysis revealed substantial between-study heterogeneity for most endpoints. Several interrelated factors likely explain this variability. Observational cohorts and registry studies reflected real-world practice with variable ascertainment and control for confounders (concomitant glucose-lowering drugs, statins, lifestyle changes). In contrast, randomized comparisons, such as post-hoc trial analyses, are less subject to treatment selection bias. Differences in design, therefore, contribute to heterogeneity. Use of sodium-glucose transport protein 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, insulin, and statins varied across studies and over time, and changes in diabetes therapy during follow-up (not always reported) can bias before-and-after comparisons. Metabolic effects may have an early incretin-mediated component and later weight- or renal-mediated effects. Therefore, studies with short versus long follow-up capture different physiologic windows. Differences in assay methods, fasting status for lipid measurements, and reporting of absolute versus relative changes further add to the variability. Because most heterogeneity was between studies (rather than within), our multilevel approach, which retained study-level clustering and performed HF-only subgroup analyses, improved interpretability and confirmed that the HbA1c reduction is consistent across the HF population.

Despite these limitations, the magnitude of HbA1c reduction observed in our pooled analysis may still be clinically meaningful in patients with diabetes or prediabetes, as such reductions are comparable to those of modest antidiabetic interventions. Notably, several randomized trials have also reported a lower rate of progression to insulin therapy among ARNI-treated patients, suggesting not only improved glycemia but also clinical relevance for therapeutic escalation [15]. For practicing clinicians, several practical points emerge. First, routine glucose and HbA1c monitoring should continue as usual after starting sacubitril/valsartan, with minor downward titration of glucose-lowering therapy considered if an individual patient shows clear improvement. Such effects could theoretically be enhanced by synergistic interactions with DPP-4 inhibition. Second, although severe hypoglycemia is uncommon, clinicians should be mindful of any potential increase in risk in patients on insulin or insulin secretagogues. Third, favorable shifts in TC, LDL, TG, HDL, and uric acid are also suggested, yet the magnitude is variable and generally modest, making them insufficient to justify changes in statin or other lipid-lowering or uric acid-lowering therapy. Therefore, standard lipid monitoring and management should be continued. Overall, the positive metabolic signal supports considering sacubitril/valsartan when metabolic comorbidities co-exist, while recognizing that these potential metabolic effects are best regarded as a possible modest bonus rather than a primary therapeutic goal.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This work has several important limitations. This study combines randomized trial sub analyses and observational records. Therefore, the observational nature and the potential for unmeasured confounding limit causal inference. Outcome measurement, reporting of concomitant diabetes and lipid therapies, and follow-up durations were heterogeneous. Hence, we were unable to perform subgroup analyses or meta-regression to adjust for these therapies, and residual confounding by concomitant glucose-lowering and hyperlipidemia treatment cannot be fully excluded. Although the metabolic effects of sacubitril/valsartan are considered to be mediated by natriuretic peptides and GLP-1, we were unable to quantitatively evaluate these mediators. Some outcomes, such as HOMA, were reported in only a small subset of studies, limiting pooled precision.

Most importantly, since our results were generated by pooling within-group MDs, the findings should be taken into consideration with caution regarding the bias and flaws attributed to this method. Furthermore, the limited number of independent studies precluded extensive meta-regression modelling without risking overfitting. Finally, as SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists are increasingly co-prescribed in HF populations, further research is needed to evaluate additive or synergistic metabolic effects and safety, including hypoglycemia risk.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this comprehensive, multilevel meta-analysis of patients receiving sacubitril/valsartan, we found a consistent reduction in HbA1c, lipid parameters, and uric acid, while insulin resistance indices showed favorable but insignificant trends. These findings, supported by randomized trial sub-analyses, observational cohorts, and mechanistic plausibility, suggest that sacubitril/valsartan may confer cardiometabolic benefits beyond hemodynamic modulation. Prospective trials with dedicated metabolic endpoints and mechanistic investigations are warranted to characterize the causality, magnitude, and clinical impact of these effects, and to guide the integration of ARNI therapy into the cardiometabolic management of HF patients.
